 SOFiMSHC is a tool for creating and processing geometric models and finite element struc- tures. SOFiMSHC can be used as stand-alone program within Teddy and is integrated as geometry processing module in the SOFiSTiK programs SOFiPLUS, Extensions for Revit and Rhinoceros Interface.
 Basis and starting point of SOFiMSHC is an abstract structural model similar to a CAD model which includes all relevant geometric and structural information necessary for describing a calculation model. After this model is read from database or entered by the user via CADINP, SOFiMSHC analyzes and processes it and creates as result a finite element mesh consisting of beam, area and/or volume elements. In addition to classical building structures, SOFiMSHC also provides a rich set of input facilities for the definition of alignment axes and bridge systems.
 SOFiMSHC basically differentiates between geometric entities carrying geometry related data and structural elements containing all further information needed for definining a calculation model. As for the geometric entities following types are supported:
 • straight lines
 circles and circular arcs in space
 alignment axes for road design defined separately in plan view and elevation
 • polygonal lines
 cubically interpolating splines
 • Hermite interpolation with defined tangents
 • arbitrary NURBS curves (Non Uniform Rational B-Splines)
 • flat surfaces
 surfaces of revolution
 •
 sweep surfaces
 bicubically interpolating surfaces
 arbitrary NURBS surfaces
 The basic geometric elements are usually defined independently from the overall structural model and should be used in as comprehensive units as possible. A bridge with multiple spans, for example, can be defined with one single axis along its whole length. The individual spans and all additional superstructures, however, are modeled with structural elements which inherit their geometry from the underlying axis definition. Once the geometry is changed the structural system will be automatically readjusted.
 The static system itself with all mutual topological relationships comprises the following set of basic structural elements:
 Structural Points are defined at a specific position in space and may have Column Heads, Punching periphery and haunches assigned as structural properties.

Once the geometry is changed the structural system will be automatically readjusted.. The static system itself with all mutual topological relationships comprises the following set of basic structural elements:. Structural Points are defined at a specific position in space and may have Column Heads, Punching periphery and haunches assigned as structural properties..
 Structural Lines connect two structural points and may have a geometric curve as- signed. Structural data includes supports and section definitions, for example.
 Structural Regions are defined by a closed set of inner and outer boundary curves and may also have a geometric surface description assigned. Structural properties contain thickness, element formulation etc.
 Structural Volumes are defined by a set of enclosing structural regions and can be meshed either unstructured with tetrahedral elements or structured by extrusion or rotation with hexahedral elements.
 A number of possibilities are provided within the SOFiSTiK program environment, to access and define the input of SOFiMSHC:
 • Definition using CADINP-ASCII-Files (Teddy + SOFiMSHC)
 Input of structural systems using SOFiPLUS (AutoCAD)
 • Transfer of models from Autodesk Revit Structural (SOFiSTiK Extensions for Revit)
 • Modeling in McNeel Rhinoceros (SOFiSTiK Rhinoceros Interface)
 • Interface to the CDBASE for third party developers and for the import of building infor- mation models (e.g. IFC).
 SOFiMSHC is both used as stand-alone batch program and as backend module in the above mentioned CAD-programs. It contains interfaces to mesh-generators from the University of Munich (DOMESH) and the University of Linz (NETGEN) and to mesh-partitioning software (METIS).

 Attention should be paid to the fact that only numbers below 1 Mio can be entered and ac- cessed within CADINP. The overall arrangement implies a **Cartesian right-handed** system in which X, Y, and Z are orthogonal.

Near the upper-right side of the diagram, there is a curved arc with a double-headed or curved arrow-like marking. This arc indicates an **angle rotation** about an axis, labeled with Greek text **“Phi_i”** (appearing as **Phi i**). Overall, the figure visually supports the explanation that SOFiMSHC uses a right-handed Cartesian X-Y-Z system, and that rotations (angles such as **Phi_i**) are defined mathematically in the positive sense with respect to the relevant local or global axis orientation.

Global as well as local coordinate systems are described in SOFiMSHC as cartesian right- handed system X-Y-Z. Rotations are applied in a mathematical positive sense. Within record SYST a global gravity direction can be specified at parameter GDIR. This global gravity or ’downward’ direction affects the default orientation of loads, supports and other geometric at- tributes of structural items within the model if not specified differently at the respective location.
 If the observer is looking from the birds eye view he will believe to see a right or left handed 2D coordinate system depending on the orientation of the vertical axis . We use the designation of the ”first” and the ”second” horizontal axis in the counter clock wise orientation.
 Each geometric or structural object in SOFiMSHC possesses a local orientation or a local coordinate system, which affects the direction of loads, cross-sections or support conditions:
 • Points, for example, have a local coordinate system which defines primarily the local di- rection of supports and kinematic couplings. If no coordinate system is given explicitly the local z-direction defaults to the globally defined gravity direction or, if the point lies within a region or on a structural line, to the local coordinate system defined there.
 • For structural lines, up to three different local coordinate systems can be identified. A first coordinate system is related to the underlying geometric curve and is primarily used to de- fine the orientation of circular arcs or alignment axes. On the structural line, an independant coordinate system can be defined which sets the orientation of cross-sections and beam elements. A third coordinate system may be specified in order to set the local direction of supports, springs or kinematic couplings connected to a line. If one of the three mentioned directions is not explicitly set by the user, it defaults to the previously defined system. If no coordinate system is defined at all, the global gravity direction is used. The local coordinate system of a structural line is normally specified by the user by setting the direction of the local z-axis. As the local x-axis always points into the direction of the curve tangent, the local y-axis is defined automatically.

If no coordinate system is defined at all, the global gravity direction is used. The local coordinate system of a structural line is normally specified by the user by setting the direction of the local z-axis. As the local x-axis always points into the direction of the curve tangent, the local y-axis is defined automatically..
 • Geometric surfaces and structural regions have a local coordinate system assigned which normally varies within the surface for curved shapes. The z-axis of the coordinate system always remains perpendicular on the surface. The coordinate system of a structural region defines, for example, the clock-order of outer boundary edges and the local orientation of the quadrilateral finite elements created on the surface.
 • For volumes there might be a direction of orthotopic material properties, but there is no local coordinate system. However all surfaces describing the volume will have a unique interior
 and exterior side. Thus a separating surface between two volumes will have a different orientation for the two cases.

Curves in SOFiMSHC are defined as parameter curves in three dimensional space. Parameter curves are basically defined by a local parameter s which runs along the curve from its start to its endpoint. A ’curve function’ c(s) maps this local parameter s to global xyz-coordinates and therefore describes the curve in space when s is changed from smin to smax:
 x(s) S>C(s)=]y(s)} S=[Smin: Smax], Z(s)
 (2.1)
 Apart from its shape other parameters might also be specified along a given curve as a func- tion of s, like for example the orientation, the size or the shape of varying cross-sections. SOFiMSHC also allows to define so-called secondary lines, which are connected to a basis curve and whose distance is defined as a function of s.

As a special type of curve SOFiMSHC allows to define alignment axes as primarily used in road and railway design. These curves typically consist of a sequence of straights and circular arcs with transition elements in between. In order to avoid sudden changes in curvature tran- sition curves (or easement curves) are placed between sections with different radii providing a gradual change of curvature from one section to another. Depending on the characteristics of the curvature gradient different types of transition elements can be identified:

 The definition of alignment axes in SOFiMSHC is carried out separately in plan view and el- evation. In plan view, sections consisting of straights, circular arcs and transition curves are combined into a sequence defining a two-dimensional curve in x,y-coordinates. The elevation of the curve can be defined independently from the plan view by setting height values and elevation radii. Curvatures in the elevation are applied as parabolas.

For defining freeform curves SOFiMSHC provides an implementaton of NURBS based on the openNURBS library. NURBS (Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines) comprise a special class of curves widely used in computer aided design or computer graphics for modelling curves and surfaces of arbitrary shapes. Mathematically, they consist of piecewise rational polynomials of a given order which are connected together under consideration of certain continuity conditions (e.g. tangentially continuous, curvature continuous). Due to their construction using rational polynomials, NURBS are also capable of representing circles, ellipses or hyperbolas mathe- matically exact. A definition of NURBS-curves basically involves the following set of properties and elements:
 The degree decribes the highest polynomial exponent of the NURBS basis functions. De- gree 1 is called linear, degree 2 quadratic, 3 cubic etc. A cubic degree is generally sufficient, but curves with degrees up to 32 may be defined and used.
 Control points are the basic construction points of a NURBS curve or surface. With ex- ception of the first and the last point they are not necessarily located directly on the curve but will stay close to it. Since NURBS curves are constructed using piecewise polyno- mials, the position of a single control point only changes the shape of its adjacent basis polynoms. This so-called ’local property’ of Nurbs - in contrast to pure polynomial curves - allows to modify a curve locally without affecting the whole shape of the curve. In addi- tion to its xyz-coordinates a control points may also have a weight assigned. By changing the control-point weights to values < > 1.0 the basis functions convert to rational polynoms which offers the possibility to model also circular arcs, hyperbolas or ellipses with NURBS.
 Basically, a single knot-value defines the location on a curve where two Nurbs basis func- tions are connected. For a given NURBS curve with N control points they are usually stored internally as monotone list of size (degree+N-1). The knot-vector may be defined by the user in order to set the local curve parametrisation explicitly. In general cases however there is no need to define the knots by the user as SOFiMSHC creates an appropriate distribution automatically. Knots can also be defined repeatedly at the same location. This knot multiplicity changes the default transition condition at the interface between two basis functions such that also kinks and even jumps could be modeled within one single curve.

SOFiMSHC supports different types of geometric surfaces which can be referenced in order to describe the shape of a structural region which is to be meshed. If no geometry is defined explicitly, SOFiMSHC tries to create the shape of a surface from its boundary description. This works, of course, for all plane surfaces and normally also for curved shapes with a less complex boundary description (e.g. four boundary edges in a rectangular like pattern). For complex shapes however, it is more reasonable to specify the geometric shape of a region explicitly.

The general idea of these type of surfaces is that a surface is defined by moving an arbitrary curve in space. In case of a surface of revolution a curve c(v) is rotated around a straight axis.
 The parametric description of the surface s(u,v) is given by
 s(,) = M() · c()
 (2.6)
 where the matrix M(v) defines rotation around an arbitrary axis in space. The parameter v denotes the rotation angle in radians. A sweep surface is defined by moving a curve c(u) along a traction curve t(v). The general form of a sweep surface s(u,v) is given by
 s(,) = t() + M() · c()
 (2.7)
 The curve c(u) may also be rotated by M(v) within the local coordinate system of the traction curve after moving it along t. In most cases however, c(v) is only translated along t(v) without rotation. The rotation matrix M defaults to the unity-matrix then.

As previously mentioned SOFiMSHC basically distinguishes between geometric entities and structural objects. Geometric elements primarily define the shape and the position of objects in space. Structural objects are referencing the shape of the geometry elements and fur- thermore contain all relevant structural information together with necessary mutual topologi- cal relationships. The structural model within SOFiMSHC corresponds to a classical B-Rep (boundary representation) data model which can be found in a similar form in other common CAD-systems. B-rep models describe objects in space by describing the boundary of the ob- jects. Structural lines, for example, are bounded by their endpoints and structural regions are bounded by a closed sequence of structural edges. Structural regions may also have internal boundaries forming openings inside the region.

The 2D-mesh generation is based on the work by Rank et al. for unstructured mesh generation for pure quadrilateral meshes. [ 1] . The first step is to generate a triangular mesh which is then divided into a quadrilateral mesh. This is the reason why along all edges the number of sections will be even.
 However there are specific macros for supports like columns modifying the basic generated mesh in a post processing step.
 The 3D-mesh generation is either done as a structured mapped mesh generation based on the surfaces generated before, or a unstructured mesh generation for pure Tetrahedron meshes. This is adopted from a mesh generator developed at the University of Linz [ 2] . SOFiSTiK programs offer the possibility to carry out all input and output of data in engineering units. Models from external CAD-systems or files often exhibit geometric inconsistencies resulting in failed meshing runs or poor element quality. SOFiMSHC provides a number of options for correction of geometry:
 In some cases basically connected curve or line sequences will be exported from external systems fragmented into multiple short structural lines. A large number of such short structural lines might increase the number of elements in the resulting finite element mesh unnecessarily. This options allows to join adjacent structural lines of similar type to single edges.
 Two neighboring lines will be connected, if the following requirements are met:
 - The length of the adjacent lines lies below the given parameter V2
 - The angle between the two lines is lower than V3
 - There is no other edge connected (no Y-joint)
 - Boundary and cross-section properties do not change.
 This options deletes openings with a surface area below the given value V2.

MESH This parameter activates the mesh generation for the defined model. Following options exist:
 0 deactivate meshing
 meshing of beam structures
 meshing of beam and shell structures
 meshing of beam, shell and/or volumes
 In addition to the basic options 1-3 one may add the following values:
 keep explicit old elements
 +32 triangular elements only
 +64 quadrilateral elements only
 +128 disable dupl. run with background mesh
 +256 post-processing only (partitioning, optim.)
 A CTRL MESH automatically activates the topological analysis and intersection of structural elements (STEU TOPO 0)
 Parameter HMIN controls globally the element size of the resulting finite element mesh. It defines the maximum allowed length of a beam and/or the edge of a
 HMIN
 shell or volume element. Please note, that the mesh density defines only an upper bound for the element size. Local geometric features or other constraints might require a smaller element size.
 In addition to the global setting, the mesh size can be overwritten individually for single structural objects (structural points, lines, regions).
 FINE Parameter FINE controls the mesh size at the corners of a structural area. Re- ducing the mesh size towards the corners usually lead to better element quality. The parameter allows two input options:
 V2>0.0 Mesh density in [ m]
 V2<0.0 Factor to general mesh density at HMIN
 EFAC This parameter controls the mesh density in the vicinity of short structural edges. In the neighborhood of short structural edges, whose length are below the global element size HMIN, the mesh density is reduced locally in order to avoid distorted quad elements with highly different edge lengths. The parameter describes the factor
 "Local mesh size" / "Length of short edge"
 Default setting is a factor of EFAC=1.40. For models containing many small edges, however, this setting might result in meshes with many local refinements, which increase the total number of elements considerably. In order to avoid the local refinements, this factor should be increased with the disadvantage, that the element quality might be reduced. On the other hand, if a model contains relatively long and small structural areas, whose width lies below the global mesh density, it is recommended to deactivate this parameter entirely (EFAC = 0). This avoids the reduction of the mesh density to the ends of the areas which results in a more regular mesh.

On the other hand, if a model contains relatively long and small structural areas, whose width lies below the global mesh density, it is recommended to deactivate this parameter entirely (EFAC = 0). This avoids the reduction of the mesh density to the ends of the areas which results in a more regular mesh..
 PROG This parameter defines the rate, how the mesh density is increased from a local refinement to the global part. It describes basically the maximum allowed ratio of the edge size between two adjacent quad elements. Standard setting is a progression factor of PROG = 1.5.

BSEC Controls the automatic generation of design sections. This option allows to gener- ate additional beam sections which will be evaluated during beam design in AQB. For example, design sections can be generated at support faces to allow for a rounding of the design moment at supports. Following options exist:
 Deactivate generation of design sections
 1
 Generate design sections at support faces along beam girders. A support will be assumed at all locations where the girder is connected to a column lying below, a wall crossing the girder or at structural points containing dimensions defined at BX,BY.
 LOCA Controls the definition of the local coordinate-system of beam elements.
 local z-axis points into gravity direction resp. the local y-axis into the first global horizontal axis if the former is not possible (i.e. beam axis parallel to gravity). User defined orientations are applied to the local y-axis.
 0
 1 local z-axis points into gravity direction resp. into the first global horizontal axis if the former is not possible (i.e. beam axis parallel to gravity). User defined orientations are applied to the local z-axis.
 2 local z-axis points into global Z resp. into global X if the former is not possible (i.e. beam axis parallel to global Z). User defined orientations are applied to the local z-axis. (Default in Industry Foundation Classes, IFC)
 3 local z-axis points into global Z resp. into global Y if the former is not possible. User defined orientations are applied to the local y-axis (GENF).
 TOLN This parameter controls the detection of double finite element nodes. FE-nodes whose distance lies below the given tolerance are intersected and replaced. The parameter is given as relative factor which will be scaled internally by model di- mensions.
 PSUP For point supports or beddings special mesh macros which reflect the geometry of the supporting column can be activated. This parameter controls this generation as follows:
 -1 no special action
 generate 4 rectangular quad elements (default)
 increase thickness of elements at support

The parameter is given as relative factor which will be scaled internally by model di- mensions.. PSUP For point supports or beddings special mesh macros which reflect the geometry of the supporting column can be activated. This parameter controls this generation as follows:. -1 no special action. generate 4 rectangular quad elements (default). increase thickness of elements at support.
 kinematic constraints of mid points
 kinematic constraints of corner points
 additional centre node for constraints
 deactivate the correction of minimum mesh size
 The kind of point support (dimensions, voute) can be set locally at the structural point property parameter SPTP.
 LSUP controls the generation of boundary elements (= supporting lines) on structural lines:
 0 create boundary elements if the line has an elastic support or contains only a group nr > 0 without a section nr.
 create boundary elements also for structural lines with rigid support in gravity direction (default setting)
 1
 2 create boundary elements if any type of support is given.
 3 create boundary elements for all edges.
 4-15 reserved for internal tests.
 +16 create elastic springs instead of boundary elements.

In order to solve the resulting equation system in the computing kernels efficiently, the equation numbers must be given in an optimized sequence. At SOFiSTiK, this optimization step is carried out during system generation on basis of the node numbers. Depending on the type of equation solver used, different kind of optimization algorithms like band-width optimization or fill-in reducing optimization are applied.
 OPTI Creates an internal numbering which allows efficient storage and solution of the resulting finite element equation system. Following options are available:
 0 deactivate optimization
 standard band-width optimization
 2 extensive band-width optimization
 +49 Fill-in reducing ordering (default)
 The type of optimization should be adapted to the equation solver to be used. An improper setting may have adverse effects. Following list shows the recom- mended settings.
 CTRL SOLV 1 band-width optimization (CTRL OPTI 1,2)
 CTRL SOLV 2 band-width optimization (CTRL OPTI 1)
 CTRL SOLV 3 Fill-in reducing ordering (CTRL OPTI 49)
 CTRL SOLV 4
 no optimization required (CTRL OPTI 0)

INIT Controls the initialisation of the system. On startup of SOFiMSHC, with the excep- tion of SYST REST, the model stored in the database is deleted and initialised. The amount of data to be deleted can be controlled using this parameter (bit- mask):
 delete stored geometric axes (GAX)
 delete stored geometric areas (GAR)
 delete stored structural elements (SPT,SLN,SAR,...)
 delete stored storey level information (SLVL)
 delete stored design elements (DECREATOR:DSLN)

The input table defines the metadata attributes of an “element group” concept used to organize structural entities (e.g., structural lines, areas, volumes) into logical sets. These groups serve as an aid for defining construction stages and for assigning loads to the correct portions of a model. The description text notes that groups must be distinguished between **primary and secondary groups**, implying that these identifiers and stage controls are foundational for that classification and for how elements participate in construction sequencing.

The table has four columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. Each row corresponds to a specific parameter that can be set per group:

1. **NO (Group number)**  
   - *Description:* A numeric identifier for the group.  
   - *Unit:* “– / LiT” (dimensionless listing/unit definition).  
   - *Default:* “!” indicating a required or special default behavior (commonly “must be provided” or triggers validation).  
   - *Role:* Establishes the unique key by which the group is referenced.

2. **REF (Span, reference or sequence number)**  
   - *Description:* A reference value representing a span number, a general reference, or a sequence number.  
   - *Unit:* “–” (dimensionless).  
   - *Default:* **0**.  
   - *Role:* Provides contextual ordering or mapping beyond the primary group identifier—useful for span-based organization or sequence tracking.

3. **BASE (Base number for this group)**  
   - *Description:* A base number used as an anchor for deriving or locating this group relative to a larger numbering scheme.  
   - *Unit:* “–”.  
   - *Default:* “*” indicating a wildcard or system-defined default behavior (e.g., inherit or auto-assign).  
   - *Role:* Supports structured numbering across multiple groups and enables consistent relationships between groups.

4. **ICS (Construction stage number of activation)**  
   - *Description:* The construction stage at which the group becomes active.  
   - *Unit:* “–”.  
   - *Default:* “-” meaning no value specified by default (inactive control or disabled).  
   - *Role:* Drives construction sequencing: elements in this group appear/participate starting at a specific stage.

5. **ICE (Construction stage number of deactivation)**  
   - *Description:* The construction stage at which the group becomes inactive.  
   - *Unit:* “– / Lit32” (dimensionless, with a listed integer format up to 32-bit).  
   - *Default:* “-” meaning deactivation stage is not set by default.  
   - *Role:* Complements activation to define a lifespan of the group across construction stages.

6. **TITL (Title of the group)**  
   - *Description:* Human-readable title/name for the group.  
   - *Unit:* “Lit32” (text field of type/size Lit32).  
   - *Default:* “-” meaning empty/not predefined.  
   - *Role:* Improves usability and traceability in model management.

Overall, the table functions as the configuration schema for group-level organization tied to construction stage activation/deactivation and numbering/reference conventions. These parameters collectively enable correct element grouping and stage-controlled behavior, supporting workflows that rely on primary/secondary group distinctions for load assignment and construction sequencing.

The input table summarizes the relationship between an **element number** and its derived **group number** under different **group divisor (GDIV)** settings. It illustrates the rule that SOFiMSHC assigns group membership using integer division of the element number by the group divisor.

### Columns
1. **Group divisor (GDIV)**
   - The table lists multiple divisor values (e.g., **1000**, **2000**, **5**).
   - GDIV is taken from the main system record **SYST** and determines how element IDs are partitioned into groups.

2. **Element number**
   - Example element numbers are shown:
     - **1**
     - **3569**
   - These are the IDs being mapped to groups.

3. **Group number**
   - The resulting computed group number for each element number under the corresponding GDIV.
   - The table includes cases where the group is “none” for element number **1** with GDIV **1000**, shown as **0 (none)**.

### Rows / Mapping examples
- With **GDIV = 1000**:
  - Element number **1** → Group number **0 (none)**
  - Element number **3569** → Group number **3**
  - This aligns with integer division behavior: values in **1000–1999** yield group 1, **2000–2999** yield group 2, and **3000–3999** yield group 3.

- With **GDIV = 2000**:
  - Element number **3569** → Group number **1**
  - Here the ranges shift: **2000–3999** map to group 1 when using division by 2000 (3569 / 2000 = 1 in integer arithmetic).

- With **GDIV = 5**:
  - Element number **3569** → Group number **713**
  - Integer division example: 3569 ÷ 5 = 713 (remainder discarded).

### Interpretation for reconstruction and storage
- The table demonstrates that group assignment is not arbitrary: it is deterministically derived from **element number** and **GDIV** using integer division.
- In the broader SOFiMSHC context (from the surrounding description), group numbers are limited (maximum group number **999**), and group base values/designations are determined automatically after generation. Large element numbers can be split into group and element parts in print outputs for readability.
- Therefore, in a RAG/vector-store setting, this table is best represented as an example of the computation rule:  
  **group_number = floor(element_number / GDIV)** with special handling where elements below the first divisible range correspond to **group 0 (none)**.

The primary group number is uniquely defined for each element. Each group is associated with a range of element numbers which easily allows to reconstruct the group id from the element id. SOFiMSHC provides different methods for the assigment of element numbers to a group. The kind of assignment is specified by the group divisor GDIV in the main system record SYST.
 The group number of a single element is defined by the integer division of the element number by the group divisor.

 The base values of all groups will be defined automatically after all elements have been generated. It is thus not any longer necessary to define base values individually. The value at GDIV < 0 defines the lowest common multiple from which the element numbers of the next higher group will be assigned to. The current limit for elements within a group is set to 1 Million.
 For all cases, the maximum group number is 999. The base number and designation is iden- tical for all elements within a group. Large element numbers will be splitted into its group and element part in print outputs in order to support better readability. It is therefor also recom- mended to use base numbers which are a multiple of 100, 1000 or 10 000.

In addition to their primary group number, elements can be assigned to any number of so called secondary groups. Secondary groups are labeled using a text string of maximum four characters (e.g. ’GR1’). The assignment of elements to secondary groups is done separately after definition of the structural system. Subsequently to the definition of the secondary group using this record any number of selection records can be given. Following type of selections are possible:
 SLN NO selection of a structural line
 SAR NO selection of a structural area
 GUID ID selection using the Globally Unique Identifier of a structural element (usually defined in a CAD-system)
 BBOX selection using a rectangular bounding box.
 Example:
 +PROG SOFIMSHC
 HEAD
 ...
 GRP NO 'GR1'
 SLN NO 1,2,3
 SAR NO 5
 ...
 END
 defines a secondary group labeled ’GR1’, which contains all beam and area elements created on the structural lines 1, 2 and 3 and structural area 5.
 Apart from this selection mechanism, elements can also be assigned to a secondary group using attribute regions. For more information please see at the description of attribute regions at record SAR.

The table describes configuration parameters for an “IMPO” record, which enables selecting meshes for 3D-extrusions from a different database. The text context indicates that this IMPO record is defined only once and then applies to all extrusion operations, so the parameters listed here act as global import/extrusion options.

The table has four columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. It appears to define three logical groups of settings: **OFT** options, plus **FROM** and **PASS** fields for specifying a database.

### 1) Item: **OFT** (Unit: “–”, Default: **0**)
The **OFT** entry is labeled **“Special options”**. It implies **OFT is an integer bit/flag-like setting** where specific values correspond to different behaviors. The table lists the following option values under the Description field:

- **0** – *no special options*  
- **1** – *convert xyz to yzx system*  
- **2** – *convert xyz to zxy system*  
- **4** – *set origin pointer to elementno*  
- **8** – *set origin pointer to elementno without group number*  
- **16** – *do not extrude support conditions*  
- **256** – *use Group instead of geometry numbers for selections*

Even though these values are shown as separate alternatives, the presence of powers of two (1,2,4,8,16,256) suggests the intent may be additive/bitmask-style; however, the table does not explicitly state combination behavior.

### 2) Item: **FROM** (Unit: **Lit96**, Default: **\***
)
The **FROM** row specifies **“Name of a database”**.  
- The **Unit** column is shown as **Lit96** (likely a literal/text type or internal token type rather than a physical unit).  
- The **Default** column is **“*”**, indicating a placeholder meaning “no fixed default” or “use provided value” (i.e., the database name must be supplied).

### 3) Item: **PASS** (Unit: **Lit16**, Default: **–**)
The **PASS** row specifies **“Password of database”**.  
- **Unit:** **Lit16** (again, an internal literal/string type indicator).  
- **Default:** **“-”**, suggesting either an empty/unspecified password by default, or that password is optional unless required by the database.

Overall, the table defines how extrusion-related import behavior is modified via **OFT** (coordinate system conversion, origin pointer handling, whether to extrude support conditions, and selection mode) and how the source data is sourced securely/explicitly via **FROM** and **PASS** fields for a specific external database.

IMPO
 With the record IMPO you may select for the 3D-extrusions the meshes to be used for the extrusion from a different database. This record may be defined only once and is then valid for all extrusions.

The table defines the parameters for an **EXPO** operation that exports record data from a database into an **input file for SOFiMSHC**. It is organized with columns **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**, indicating both the configurable settings and what values are expected or assumed when not explicitly provided.

### Item: OPT (required setting category; “Data to be exported”)
- **Description:** Specifies the *type and extent* of data exported.
- **Options listed in the Description cell:**
  - **GAX**: *Geometric axis* elements.
  - **GAR**: *Geometric surface* elements.
  - **RAW**: *Basic structural model* export (minimal/default dataset).
  - **FULL**: *Extended properties* export.
- **Unit column:** shows **LIT** (a literal/value-type indicator rather than a physical unit).
- **Default:** **RAW**, meaning that if OPT is not set, the export will include the basic structural model.

**Behavior relevance from context:** If an **Identifier** is additionally given at **GAX** or **GAR**, only the selected axis/surface is exported; otherwise, all elements of the chosen type are exported. Using **FULL** adds internal/export-only details such as internally used datatypes and **globally unique identifiers (GUIDs)** of structural elements, enabling identification of structural objects across different CAD systems.

### Item: VAL (optional selector/identifier)
- **Description:** **ID of axis or surface (optional)**.
- **Unit column:** **Lit4**, indicating an expected literal-like identifier type.
- **Default:** **“-”**, meaning no default value is implied; it is optional.
- **Purpose:** When OPT is **GAX** or **GAR**, VAL can narrow the export to a specific geometric entity by its ID.

### Item: TO (output file name)
- **Description:** **Name of a file to write to**.
- **Unit column:** **Lit96** (literal/value type).
- **Default:** **“*”**.
- **Context mapping:** If no file name is specified, the export defaults to **`project_MEX.dat`**. (The table’s “*” default symbol indicates the parameter supports an implicit default behavior.)

### Item: PASS (database password)
- **Description:** **Password of database**.
- **Unit column:** **Lit16** (literal/value type).
- **Default:** **“-”**, indicating no password is provided by default (or that the field is expected to be omitted/left blank unless needed).

### Overall meaning
Collectively, this parameter set controls **what** geometry/structure is exported (**OPT**), **which specific geometry** may be selected (**VAL**), **where** the output is written (**TO**), and **whether authentication** is required (**PASS**). The export is subsequently written using the **current unit settings from record PAGE** for numeric values, and the **language of the new file matches the current CADINP input file**.

EXPO
 Using record EXPO geometric or structural elements within the database can be exported into an input file for SOFiMSHC. This can be useful when analyzing the data after an error occured or to make further use of the data in different settings.
 If an Identifier is given additionally at GAX or GAR, only the selected geometric axis or surface is exported to the file, otherwise all elements of the given type are exported. When using option FULL, additional properties of the model are exported, including internally used datatypes and globally uniqe identifiers (GUID) of the structural elements, which will be used for idenfication of structural objects in different CAD-systems.
 If no file name is specified the data will be exported to a file named project_MEX.dat.
 The units of the values will be set to the current setting of UNIE from record PAGE. The lan- guage of the new file will be the same as the current CADINP input file.

The input table defines parameters for an output-control command or function that generates different types of model data and reporting. It has four columns: **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**. Two configuration fields are shown: **OPT** and **VAL**. Both use the unit/format type **LIT** (literal/string-like selection) and default to **FULL**, meaning “no restriction” unless overridden.

## Item: OPT (Output options)
- **Purpose:** Selects *what categories* of information the command should output.  
- **Type/Unit:** **LIT**  
- **Default:** **FULL**

**OPT** accepts a **literal** from a predefined list:
- **MAT** – *Material data*
- **SECT** – *Section for beams*
- **GEOM** – *Geometric items*
- **NODE** – *Generated nodes*
- **QUAD** – *Generated quadrilaterals*
- **BRIC** – *Generated volume elements*
- **BEAM** – *Generated beam elements*
- **BOUN** – *Generated elastic supports*
- **SYST** – *System summary*
- **STAT** – *Analysis statistics*

Additionally, **OPT** may be set to:
- **FULL** – enables **all the above options**.

Context note (from the additional text): **ECHO-Option SYST** corresponds specifically to the system summary and may be defined either with named presets (**NO/YES/FULL/EXTR**) or as a **numerical bitpattern**. The bitpattern selects finer-grained breakdowns (e.g., primary group statistics, beam/truss/cable statistics, area/volume element statistics, ordering by various groupings, reinforcements sums, nodal masses, life-cycle assessment, element-type LCA, etc.). This suggests that “SYST” output can be extended beyond a simple on/off choice.

## Item: VAL (Value of output option)
- **Purpose:** Controls the **verbosity level** or intensity of output for the selected OPT categories.
- **Type/Unit:** **LIT**  
- **Default:** **FULL**

Allowed values:
- **NO** – no output
- **YES** – regular output
- **FULL** – extensive output
- **EXTR** – extreme output

## Overall behavior implied by the table
- **OPT** chooses *which domains* to report (materials, geometry, generated entities, system summary, statistics).
- **VAL** chooses *how much* to report for those domains (none → regular → extensive → extreme).
- The defaults for both fields are **FULL**, so unless the caller specifies otherwise, the command will (a) include all OPT categories and (b) produce extensive verbosity.

See also:
 ECHO
 The name (ECHO) of this record must be repeated every time the command is being used, otherwise it may be confused with other records with the same name.

 respectively by structural members for design elements

 (not for design elements)

This table defines **COOR** (record “COOR / T23 0.0”), i.e., the **type and parameters of a reference coordinate system** used by SOFiMSHC for interpreting subsequent **position and direction inputs** in certain structural records.

## Purpose and scope
- After **COOR** sets a coordinate system, all **subsequent structural point/line/area definitions** that specify **positions (X,Y,Z)** or **directions (DX,DY,DZ)** are interpreted according to the chosen coordinate system.
- The coordinate system may be changed **within a data record** as often as needed.
- **COOR WRLD** resets the interpretation to the default **world Cartesian system** (Euclidean, origin at **(0,0,0)**).
- The coordinate system affects only:
  - **Structural element records and their property records**, specifically referenced in context as **SPT, SLN, SAR**.
- The coordinate system for **geometry input** (e.g., **GAX, GAR**) **cannot be changed** by COOR.

## Key items/fields
### TYPE (default: `WRLD`, unit: `LIT`)
Selects the reference system type / how COOR is established:
- `WRLD`: world coordinate system
- `SPT`: referenced to a structural point
- `AXIS`: referenced to an axis
- `GAXP`: referenced to a placement
- `CYLI`: cylindrical coordinate system
- `SPHE`: spherical coordinate system

### ID (default: `- / Lit8`)
An identifier for the referenced object, whose meaning depends on **TYPE**:
- For `SPT`: structural point number
- For `AXIS`: axis reference (possibly including secondary axis forms like `A1.B`)
- For other types it provides the “number/ID of reference item” as indicated.

### IDP (default: `Lit4`)
Placement identifier used when **TYPE = GAXP**.
- Provides the **ID of the placement**, as an alternative to identifying the placement by its station position (described in the context text).

### S
Station/parameter on an axis (used for `AXIS` or `GAXP`-type referencing), described as:
- “Parameter on axis (Typ AXIS, GAXP)”
- Unit is not explicitly shown for this column in the excerpt, but it is described as a parameter on an axis.

### X, Y, Z (origin coordinates; default: `0.0`)
Define the **origin** of the coordinate system at coordinates:
- `X`: coordinate of origin
- `Y`: coordinate of origin (for coordinate types where Y is valid as origin coordinate)
- `Z`: coordinate of origin
- Units for these are shown as **meters** (`[m]`) with default **0.0**.

### Direction vectors T11–T23 (orientation; defaults given)
Used to define the orientation for systems based on explicit Cartesian axes:
- `T11, T12, T13`: first local axis direction vector (**local T1**)
  - default shown: T11=1.0, T12=0.0, T13=0.0
- `T21, T22, T23`: second local axis direction vector (**local T2**)
  - default shown: T21=0.0, T22=1.0, T23=0.0

**Derived behavior (from context):**
- The **third axis** is computed as the **cross product** of the first and second axes.
- If T2 is not orthogonal to T1, COOR **orthogonalizes** the system before deriving the third direction.

## Coordinate-type-specific interpretation (from context)
- **Orthogonal/axis-based Cartesian systems:** origin at (X,Y,Z), orientation defined by T1 and T2.
- **SPT / AXIS:** the coordinate system is moved/rotated into the local coordinate system of the referenced structural point or station on an axis.
- **GAXP (placement):** local axes align with the **cut-plane** of the placement; the “local z” typically points into gravity direction. Additionally, when defining coordinate system via GAXP, **beam elements become aligned perpendicular to the placement plane** (local z oriented toward the coordinate system’s x-axis).
- **CYLI (cylindrical):** subsequent inputs interpret:
  - X = radial distance from rotational axis
  - Y = azimuth angle in rotational plane
  - Z = height along rotational axis
- **SPHE (spherical):** subsequent inputs interpret:
  - X = radius from origin
  - Y = azimuth angle (phi) in equatorial plane
  - (and an inclination from equatorial plane, as described in the context text)

Overall, this table provides the complete parameterization needed for defining how **future structural definitions** interpret spatial coordinates and directions under a selectable coordinate reference framework.

The table describes the parameter schema for the **XSUB** record used to create a **submodel (subsystem) extracted from a general structural model** for detailed independent analysis. It specifies the **type of submodel** and the **treatment of stiffness at cut connections** by mapping the degrees of freedom of adjacent/connected structural elements to equivalent boundary conditions using spring elements or fixed supports.

**Columns**
- **Item**: Parameter keyword (e.g., TYPE, FIXA).
- **Description**: Meaning of the parameter.
- **Unit**: Expected unit or value form. Here, stiffness control parameters use a generic literal/type format `- / Lit` (indicating either a literal keyword or a numeric factor).
- **Default**: Default value if the parameter is omitted.

### Parameters

1. **TYPE (Unit: Lit4; Default: SPAC)**
   - Sets the **system type of the submodel**:
     - `3D` = spatial 3D system.
     - `SLAB` = 2D plate/girder system.
   - Context: If extracted as `SLAB` (plate), the selected structural elements are projected onto the **xy-plane at z = 0.0**.

2. **FIXA (Unit: /Lit; Default: FIX)**
   - Controls **axial stiffness** of connected elements.
   - Accepts:
     - a **numeric value** > 0.0 interpreted as a **factor** multiplying computed default axial stiffness, or
     - the literal `FIX` (fully fixed support), or
     - the literal `FREE` (release the corresponding degrees of freedom).
   - Context for default stiffness computation: axial bedding uses formulas based on connected element type:
     - For a structural line: \( c = E \cdot A / l \)
     - For a structural area: \( c = E \cdot b / h \)

3. **FXIL (Unit: /Lit; Default: 1.0)**
   - Controls **lateral stiffness**.
   - Same interpretation rules as other FIX* parameters:
     - numeric factor scales computed lateral stiffness,
     - `FIX` enforces fixed behavior,
     - `FREE` releases DOFs.
   - Context: lateral stiffness is computed assuming hinged support at the bottom, with separate expressions for structural lines (using \(E I_y\) / \(l^3\)) or structural areas (using \(E i_y\) / \(h^3\)).

4. **FXIM (Unit: /Lit; Default: 0.0)**
   - Controls **rotational stiffness** at connections.
   - Numeric values act as scaling factors; literals `FIX`/`FREE` enforce or release rotational DOFs.
   - Context: rotational stiffness is also computed under hinged-support assumptions:
     - for structural lines: \( c_r = 3EI / l \)
     - for structural areas: \( c_r = 3E i_y / h \)

5. **FXIS (Unit: /Lit; Default: 1.0)**
   - Controls **shear stiffness** for adjacent walls/slabs.
   - Interpretation: numeric scaling of default shear stiffness, or use `FIX`/`FREE`.
   - Context: shear stiffness for structural areas is given by:
     - \( k_s = G \cdot b / h \)
   - Applied along the boundary edge in longitudinal direction.

6. **CDB (Unit: Lit; Default: (blank/not specified))**
   - Specifies **name of the file to be created** for the extracted submodel database.

### Overall meaning
Together, these parameters define:
- what kind of extracted system is produced (**3D vs SLAB/plate projection**),
- and how structural stiffness is approximated at cut interfaces via spring constants with controllable axial/lateral/rotational/shear behavior using `FIXA–FIXS`, with explicit defaults for each stiffness component.

 XSUB
 This records allows to extract a partial system from a general structural model for a detailed analysis. The extracted model will be stored in a new database as planar slab or again as new spacial system, which can be then meshed and calculated in a separate independent project.
 In the case, that the partial model will be extracted as plate system (TYPE SLAB) all selected structural elements will be projected onto the xy-plane at coordinate z=0.0.
 All structural elements connected to the partial model which will be cut during the extraction, like adjacent columns or walls, will be replaced by linear elastic spring elements or fixed sup- ports approximating the stiffness at the connection. The generation of these boundary condi- tions can be controlled using the parameters FIXA to FIXS. The four parameters distinguish between axial, lateral, rotational and shear stiffness components.
 The bedding component in axial direction of connected elements will be calculated as fol- lows:
 Connected Structural line c = E*A/l
 Structural area: c = E*b/h
 ’A’ denotes the cross section area and ’l’ the length of the connected structural line (e.g. column). For adjacent structural areas the linear elastic distributed bedding replacing the area will be calculated from the thickness b and the average height/width h of the connected wall/slab.
 The stiffness in transversal direction will be calculated under the assumption, that the con- nected building element has hinged support at the bottom:
 Structural line:
 c = 3 * E Iy / l3 (bzw. 3 * E Iz / l3)
 c = 3 * E iy / h3
 Structural area:
 For an adjacent structural line two spring elements will be created for the stiffness in the direction of the local y- and z-axis of the cross section. For a connected structural region, the lateral bedding is calculated by the distributed moment of intertia iy = b3 / 12 and the medial height/width of the region.

For an adjacent structural line two spring elements will be created for the stiffness in the direction of the local y- and z-axis of the cross section. For a connected structural region, the lateral bedding is calculated by the distributed moment of intertia iy = b3 / 12 and the medial height/width of the region..
 For the computation of the rotational stiffness, it is again assumed, that the connected building element has hinged support at the bottom:
 Structural line: cr = 3 * E Iy / l (bzw. 3 * E Iz / l)
 Structural area: cr = 3 * E iy / h
 For adjacent walls or slabs the shear stiffness will be calculated as follows:
 Structural area ks = G * b / h
 The stiffness is applied in longitudinal direction along the connected boundary edge.
 In all four cases, a numerical value > 0.0 or one of the two literals FIX or FREE can be given at FIXA to FIXS. In the case, that a numerical value is given, it will be interpreted as factor multiplying the default stiffness values calculated as given above. The literal ’FIX’ creates a fixed support and the literal ’FREE’ releases the respective degrees of freedom entirely.
 The elements of the partial system are selected by entering subsequent records directly after XSUB:
 • SLN: Selection of a structural line with number NO
 • SAR: Selection of a structural region with number NO
 • GUID: Selection using a Globally Unique Identifier (GUID) A GUID uniquely identifies a structural element and will be usually set when exporting the model from a CAD system (e.g. SOFiPLUS, Extensions for Revit).
 • BBOX: Selection using a rectangular bounding box This option is especially suitable for selecting all structural elements on a specified floor level (e.g. BBOX z1 9.5 z2 10.5).
 The selection records given above can be defined in any number and any order.

The table documents the input parameters of a record (referenced in the context as the CadInp “subsystem extraction” control record, related to prior definition at **XSUB** and followed by an element selection/control at **XCON**). Its purpose is to fine-tune **support conditions** that will be generated for elements **connected** to a previously extracted subsystem. Conceptually, the record does not select the subsystem itself; instead, it controls how supports are created for a specific subsequent **element selection** in relation to that subsystem, including what stiffness components are applied.

### Columns
- **Item**: Parameter name as used in the input deck.
- **Description**: Human-readable meaning of the parameter.
- **Unit**: Displayed unit/scale notation. Values are expressed as **“–/Lit”**, and the meaning is that the specified value acts as a **type or factor** using the logical length factor “Lit” (or scaling convention “Lit” used by the software). The “Unit” column is therefore not a physical unit like N/m, but a parameterization/scale format.
- **Default**: Default value when the parameter is not explicitly provided.

### Parameters (rows)

1. **SEL** (Selection)  
   Defines which building members are relevant when generating support conditions with respect to the subsystem. Two selection keywords are listed:
   - **ABOV**: selects **building members lying above the subsystem**.
   - **BELO**: selects members **below the subsystem**.
   
   The table shows **Unit: Lit4** and **Default: “-”** (no default). This implies the user must specify whether to target above or below.

2. **FIXA** (Type or factor of axial stiffness)  
   Controls the **axial** stiffness contribution used to model the support at connected elements in the axis direction.  
   - **Default: `FIX`**  
   - This indicates a “fixed”/full axial stiffness mode unless overridden.

3. **FIXL** (Type or factor of lateral stiffness)  
   Controls the **lateral** stiffness (horizontal/sideways) of the support springs or stiffness model.  
   - **Default: `1.0`**  
   - Interpreted as a scaling factor (relative stiffness).

4. **FIXM** (Type or factor of rotational stiffness)  
   Controls the **rotational** stiffness (moment/rotation resistance) of the support.  
   - **Default: `0.0`**  
   - Meaning that by default, rotational restraint is not applied unless the user sets it otherwise.

5. **FIXS** (Type or factor of shear stiffness)  
   Controls the **shear** stiffness contribution.  
   - **Default: `1.0`**  
   - The context further notes that shear stiffness is only used for **connected walls and slabs**, not necessarily for all element types.

### Overall significance for RAG use
This table provides the exact parameter set needed to reproduce the support-condition generation behavior: first choose whether to apply support logic to elements **above or below** the subsystem (**SEL**), then specify which stiffness components are applied at connected elements (**FIXA/FIXL/FIXM/FIXS**) and how strongly (defaults given), including the special handling of shear stiffness for walls and slabs.

### Table/Record Description: **GAX (Geometry Axis)**
This record defines an **alignment axis** used in SOFiMSHC for road design and arbitrary geometric curves. It is designed to be largely **independent of structural elements**, serving as a **central geometric reference** from which dependent components can be defined. A key concept is that once the **axis geometry is modified**, all structures that reference this axis can be **automatically adapted**.

In bridge design, for example, the bridge geometry can be expressed relative to a single master axis: supports, girders, varying cross-sections, additional load lines, or secondary girders can be derived from it. The record also supports defining **variable distributions along the axis** (via related secondary-axis and variable-definition records).

Additionally, geometry axes support multiple curve definition approaches (via the geometry type parameter and subsequent curve-type sub-records). Curve definitions can also be created **relative to another previously defined curve** (enabling offset or copy behavior), and curves may be **projected onto surfaces** or generated as **intersections of two surfaces**.

---

## Fields in the table

- **ID** *(Lit4, default “!”)*:  
  Identifier for the axis. The system restricts this to **literal strings of up to four characters** (e.g., `GAX ID 'AX1'`). This ID is the primary key used by other records to reference the axis.

- **TYPE** *(LIT, default “LANE”)*:  
  Determines the semantic type of the axis. Allowed values include:
  - `DEL`: delete this entry  
  - `NONE`: no specific type  
  - `AXIS`: system axis (e.g., “A-A”)  
  - `BEAM`: axis of a beam sequence  
  - `LANE`: traffic lane  
  - `TEND`: tendon axis  

- **ID2**, **ID3**, **ID4**:  
  Reserved for **export of additional data** (no functional meaning in the core definition).

- **ID5** *(default 1)*:  
  Another reserved/export-related field; default is `1`.

- **REF** *(Lit4, default “-”)*:  
  Reference to a **master axis**. When set, the current axis can be derived from or associated with another axis (e.g., for hierarchical definitions).

- **SUR1** *(Lit4)*:  
  Number/identifier of a **geometric surface**. Used for projecting a generated curve onto a surface.

- **SUR2** *(Lit4)*:  
  Number/identifier of a **second geometric surface**. If provided together with `SUR1`, the generated curve corresponds to the **intersection line** of the two surfaces.

- **TYPC** *(LIT)*:  
  Type of curve to be generated for the axis. The record schema indicates that curve generation is linked to other GAXC-type mechanisms.

- **DEGR** *(default “-”)*:  
  Degree of the spline curve (explicitly referenced as “see **GAXC**”). This is relevant when the curve type involves spline interpolation (e.g., B-splines/NURBS-related definitions).

- **TITL** *(Lit32)*:  
  Human-readable designation/title of the axis.

While **GAX** establishes the axis definition container and metadata, the actual **geometry is generated by subsequent records**. Typical geometry sub-record types (noted in the provided context) include:
- `AXIS` (GAXA / GAXH): alignment axes in plan and elevation  
- `ARC` (GAXB): 3D lines and circular arcs

### Table: **GAXA parameter record for alignment axis sections (plan view)**

This table defines the fields of the **record “GAXA”**, which is a *property record* used to specify how an alignment axis section should be constructed in **plan view**. It must follow a preceding axis definition at **GAX**. The record provides either a **length-based** segment sequence definition or a **tangential/polygon-based** definition that SOFiMSHC converts into curves with appropriate geometry transitions.

The table lists the following items, together with their meaning, unit, and default values:

- **S (Station value)**  
  Indicates the station position for the start of this defined section. Unit is not specified (shown as “—”). Default is `*` meaning a value must be provided.

- **X (Coordinates of startpoint / tangential intersection point)**  
  Gives the x-coordinate for either:
  - the startpoint in the length-based definition, or
  - the tangential intersection point in the tangentially based definition.  
  Unit: **m**, Default: `*`.

- **Y (Coordinates of startpoint / tangential intersection point)**  
  Corresponding y-coordinate. Unit: **m**, Default: `*`.

- **SX (Direction of tangent, x-component)**  
  Defines the tangent direction component associated with the startpoint. Unit: **—**, Default: `*`.

- **SY (Direction of tangent, y-component)**  
  Defines the tangent direction y-component. Unit: **—**, Default: `*`.

- **L (Length of section)**  
  Length of the axis section to be created. Unit: **m**, Default: `*`.

- **R (Radius)**  
  Radius of curvature for the circular (arc) part of the curve sequence. Unit: **m**, Default: `*`.  
  Sign convention (from the context): **positive** radius creates curvature to the **right-hand side**, **negative** creates curvature to the **left-hand side**.

- **RA (Radius of the axis at start)**  
  Radius at the beginning of the curve sequence (supports varying radius between start and end). Unit: **m**, Default: `R`.  
  If not specified, it equals the main radius `R`, implying continuous curvature matching at the start.

- **RE (Radius of the axis at end)**  
  Radius at the end of the curve sequence. Unit: **m**, Default: `R`.

- **LA (Length of first transition element)**  
  Length of the first transition element (e.g., clothoid) between straight/tangent and circular arc. Unit: **m**.  
  Default: `*` (no value auto-assumed).  
  Context note: `< 0` is allowed and indicates an alternative parameterization for clothoids (R*L = A²).

- **LE (Length of second transition element)**  
  Length of the second transition element. Unit: **m**.  
  Default: `LA`, meaning if the second transition length is not specified, it defaults to the first.  
  Same clothoid parameterization note applies: `< 0` indicates R*L = A² behavior.

- **TYPS (Type of transition curve)**  
  Selects the mathematical form of the transition curve between tangents and circular arcs. Unit: “LIT”.  
  Default: **CLOT** (clothoid).

All length/coordinate-related parameters use **meters [m]** (shown as **[m]1001**), while chainage/parametrisation parameters use unit “—”.

### General role of the record
A **GAXB** record defines one or more **curve segments** along a previously defined **axis at GAX**. Multiple segments can be provided to form polycurves. When multiple segments are combined, the transitions should be **smooth**: the tangents at the shared point should be **continuous**. Kinks are allowed but discouraged because they can cause meshing problems; if a kink is required, the guidance is to split the geometry into two curves with a **structural point** between them.

### Geometry definition parameters
The table lists the numeric inputs needed depending on the chosen segment type:

- **R (Radius)**: The circle/arc radius. Unit: **[m]1001**. Default: “-” (implies required when applicable).
- **XM, YM, ZM (Coordinates of center)**: Center point of the circle/arc. Each has unit **[m]1001**.

- **X2, Y2, Z2 (Endpoint)**: Endpoint of a **straight** segment or a circular arc. Units **[m]1001**.
- **X3, Y3, Z3 (Third point on circular arc)**: An additional point lying on the arc used to define an arc via **three points**. Units **[m]1001**.

These parameters support multiple alternative arc/line definitions (as also stated in the context text):  
- Straight line: by **(X1,Y1,Z1)** and **(X2,Y2,Z2)**.

The table describes the **per-point definition fields** of the geometry record **GAXC**, which is used to define **individual points on a freeform 3D curve**. Each **GAXC record contributes one coordinate** (a datapoint) to the curve geometry that is defined in the preceding/main axis record (**GAX**). The interpretation of these point coordinates depends on the curve type and parameters specified in the main record, but the fields listed here are the inputs for the datapoints themselves.

### Columns
- **Item**: Field name within the GAXC point record.
- **Description**: Meaning of the field and how it influences the curve.
- **Unit**: Measurement unit for that field.
- **Default**: Default value used when the parameter is omitted.

### Fields and their roles
1. **X (3D coordinates, [m], default 0.0)**  
   The global or local **X coordinate** of the curve datapoint. In cases where the main record GAX references another axis (**REF**), X is reinterpreted as **station/chainage S** along the reference axis (per the provided context).

2. **Y (3D coordinates, [m], default 0.0)**  
   The **Y coordinate** of the datapoint (global), or—under **REF** mode—the **distance offset** from the reference axis measured in the referenced local coordinate system.

3. **Z (3D coordinates, [m], default 0.0)**  
   The **Z coordinate** of the datapoint (global), or—under **REF** mode—the **distance offset** along the reference axis local coordinate system.

4. **W (weight of control point for NURBS, unitless, default 1.0)**  
   NURBS-specific parameter defining the **weight** of the control point.  
   - If **W ≠ 1.0**, the curve becomes a **rational NURBS**, enabling more accurate conic representations such as **circles and ellipses**.
   - **W = 1.0** corresponds to a non-rational (standard) B-spline behavior for that point.

5. **S (Stati(on)/chainage on point for interpolation, unitless, default '-' meaning none)**  
   Optional **parametrization value** for the datapoint used during curve construction. It controls where along the curve the point lies in the parameter domain (“chainage”). If omitted, the system assigns parametrization automatically; in such cases, the **end chainage corresponds to geometric axis length**.

6. **DX, DY, DZ (tangential direction, each unitless, default '-')**  
   Optional directional components used to explicitly define the **tangent direction** at the point (marked as Type HINT in the context). These are especially relevant when the curve type uses **tangential (C1) continuity**, where the user can steer tangent behavior at selected points.

7. **NX, NY, NZ (direction/orientation of local z-axis, not available, unitless, default '-')**  
   Intended to set a user-defined **orientation of the curve’s local z-axis** at the point, allowing arbitrarily oriented cross-sections along the curve. In this table, these fields are marked **“not available”**, implying they are either unsupported in the current configuration or not exposed in this interface. The context also states that if no directions are given, the local z-axis defaults to pointing toward the **globally defined gravity direction**.

### Relationship to curve construction (from context)
- GAXC points are connected into the curve according to interpolation mode defined in **GAX** and by parameters such as **TYPC** and **DEG**.  
- Depending on the selected type, points may be:
  - connected by a polygonal line,
  - interpolated with a **cubic B-spline (C2 continuity)**,
  - interpolated with **piecewise cubic B-spline segments (C1 continuity)** using optional tangents (DX/DY/DZ),
  - or used as **NURBS control points** using weights **W** and NURBS degree/knots.
- If **REF** is provided in GAX, the meaning of X/Y/Z shifts from absolute coordinates to reference-axis station and local offsets.

Overall, the table specifies the **numeric inputs available per curve datapoint** for GAXC, covering geometry location (X/Y/Z), NURBS weighting (W), interpolation parametrization (S), optional tangent direction (DX/DY/DZ), and (theoretically) local cross-section orientation via NX/NY/NZ.

See also: GAX, GAXN, GAXP, GAXS, GAXV

The points always refer to the directly preceding geometry axis. The type and the degree of the curve is specified by the parameters TYPC and DEG within the main record GAX:
 The given points will be connected to a polygonal line.
 The given datapoints will be interpolated using a cubic B-Spline. The interpolation is carried out curvature continuous at the definition points (C2-continuity).
 The chainage (parametrisation) of the curve can be set explicitly at each datapoint using the parameter S. If no parameter values are given, SOFiMSHC assigns a parametrisation automatically. The end chainage corresponds to the geometric length of the axis in this case.

Using the parameters DX,DY,DZ, the tangential direction at certain points can be defined explicitly by the user. Similar to the spline interpolation, the parametrisation (chainage) along the curve can be set using the parameter S.
 A NURBS (Non Uniform Rational B-Spline) curve can be defined by entering the euclidian coordinates of the control-points at X,Y,Z. If weights < > 1.0 are given, the input results in a true ’rational’ NURBS curve, which, for example, allows to describe also circle and ellipses. If a reference axis REF is given in the main record GAX, the X-values are then interpreted as station value S on the reference axis and the values Y and Z as distances relatively to the local coordinate system of the referenced axis. The thus defined points are then interpolated by a cubic B-spline (TYPC SPLI).  At NX,NY,NZ a user defined orientation of the local z-axis can be set for each point on the curve independantly. The table defines the **record layout for item type `GAXN`**, which is used in SOFiMSHC to control the **knot vector** of NURBS curves and/or to set the **parametrization of interpolation curves**. Conceptually, `GAXN` entries provide the knot parameter values and their multiplicities, referencing a previously defined geometry axis (via `GAX`) that establishes the curve’s coordinate/parameter system.

### Purpose and usage
- For a NURBS curve, **each knot value** (or each relevant parameter value for an interpolation curve) is represented by an individual `GAXN` record.
- Each record corresponds to a knot value and specifies the **multiplicity** for that knot.
- Multiple occurrences at the same knot location (e.g., at the curve ends) are expressed via **multiplicity > 1** in a single record rather than repeating separate records.
- In the **first `GAXN` record**, the **polynomial degree** of the NURBS curve can be set using `DEGR`. This implies that `DEGR` is a curve-wide parameter that is only needed/processed on the initial knot definition record.
- When defining NURBS curves in SOFiMSHC, the knot vector typically must follow NURBS conventions with **clamped ends**: the end knots must have multiplicity equal to the **degree** of the curve. If the user provides no knot vector at all, the system assumes a **uniform knot distribution** internally.

### Table fields
The table lists four columns that describe the structure of `GAXN` records:

1. **Item**
   - Identifies the parameter name used in the record.

2. **Description**
   - Explains the meaning of each item.

3. **Unit**
   - Indicates that these fields are not physical units; knot/degree parameters are dimensionless. The table shows “–” for Unit.

4. **Default**
   - Provides default values when not explicitly specified.

### Fields in detail
- **`S` – Knot value**
  - **Meaning:** The actual knot parameter value (a scalar) for the NURBS/interpolation definition.
  - **Default:** marked with `!` indicating **required input** (no default).
  - **Role:** This value determines where along the parameter domain the knot is placed.

- **`MUL` – Multiplicity**
  - **Meaning:** How many times the knot value is repeated in the knot vector.
  - **Default:** `1`
  - **Role:** Higher multiplicity affects continuity properties at that knot (e.g., ensuring endpoint interpolation with clamped knots by using multiplicity equal to degree).

- **`DEGR` – degree of Nurbs**
  - **Meaning:** The polynomial degree of the NURBS curve.
  - **Default:** `1`
  - **Role:** Typically set in the **first `GAXN` record** to define the curve degree used for interpreting the knot vector, especially for determining required end multiplicities (clamped ends).

Overall, this table specifies the minimal control parameters (`S`, `MUL`, `DEGR`) needed to construct the knot vector for NURBS curves (or set interpolation parametrization), with `DEGR` applied at the start and `S/MUL` defining the sequence of knot entries tied to an earlier `GAX` geometry axis definition.

The table defines the input fields for **GAXP (Placements along a geometry axis)**. A *placement* establishes an **infinite plane** at a given **station S** perpendicular to the axis tangent. The model then creates **structural points** (and related structural lines/elements) on the primary and/or secondary axes at the intersections of this plane with the axes. The placement type also drives special behavior for structural system generation (e.g., supports and endfaces).

## Main identity and axis selection
- **ID (Lit4)**: Identifies the **primary axis** the placement belongs to.
- **IDS (LIT)**: Selects which **secondary axes** are affected. Accepted literal meanings are:
  - `0` = primary axis only
  - `A-Z` = secondary axes (with “A-Z” indicating the axis range naming convention)
  - `*,` = all axes
  - `,+'` = only secondary axes (excluding primary)

## Station and placement classification
- **S ( /Lit)**: The **station value** along the axis. It may be given as a numeric station or **as a variable name** (in which case placements are created for each base-point of that variable).
- **TYPE (Lit8)**: Placement type, given as a character literal:
  - `'S'` support
  - `'J'` construction joint
  - `'A'` startface
  - `'E'` endface
  - `'H'` horizontal connection  
  The context notes that placements are typically defined as combinations of literals at **TYP** (e.g., `'SJ'`), and that enclosing literals in apostrophes avoids ambiguity. The chosen type also affects how internal span-related parameters (such as curve parameter mapping between supports) are established for support/start/endface types.

## Structural point and sectioning control
- **SPT**: The **structural point number** to create at this placement.
  - If **not specified**, the system assigns values automatically (context: starting at **SPT=1000** in **intervals of 100**), and recommends increasing the automatic start via parameter **CTRL NODE** to avoid collision with user-defined numbering.
- **GRP (default 0)**: **Group number** for the subsequent section elements.
- **NCS (default 0)**: Controls **cross-section numbering** for subsequent beam/structural elements. It can be given directly as a cross-section number or as a relative form around the placement: `ncs1.ncs2` (interpreted as “number before/after placement”).
  - The system’s beam-element generation starts at the **first placement that has a cross-section assigned** and ends at the axis end or at a placement of type `'E'` (endface).

- **IDP**: Unique **identifier of the placement**. This enables referencing the placement in later computation steps (e.g., when recording coordinates).

## Local positioning and alignment (geometry offsets/rotations)
These fields affect the placement’s geometry orientation and intersection-related point creation:
- **Y (m, default 0.0)**: Additional explicit **transverse offset** in local **y**.
- **Z (m, default 0.0)**: Additional explicit **vertical offset** in local **z**.
- **ALF (deg)**: Alignment about the **global Z direction** (angle 1–360° mentioned in context).
- **ALFX, ALFY, ALFZ (deg, defaults 0.0)**: Rotations (“skew”) about local axes:
  - **ALFX**: skew about local x-axis
  - **ALFY**: skew about transverse y-axis
  - **ALFZ**: skew about vertical z-axis
- **INCR**: Cross fall to the right **(+y)**.
- **INCL**: Cross fall to the left **(−y)** (default is expressed as the negative of INCR in the table).
  - Context notes that cross-fall sign follows height change direction outward, and that angle-based inclination variables **#INCR/#INCL** can be used in some situations (they represent clockwise radians about X-axis rather than a tangent value).

The table documents **GAXS**, a command that defines a **secondary axis** relative to an existing **primary axis**. In the context provided, the secondary axis spacing can be specified either as a **constant offset** in the local **y** and **z** directions, or as a **variable-dependent distance** using **GAXV**. It also supports adjusting numbering offsets for **structural points** and **group numbers** associated with related **GAXP** placements. Additionally, related commands are referenced: **GAX**, **GAXP**, **GAXV**, and **GAXS** itself.

The table has columns **Item**, **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default**, listing the parameters required or supported by GAXS:

- **ID** (“Ident of Primary axis”)  
  Identifies which primary axis the secondary axis is derived from.  
  **Unit:** `LIt4`  
  **Default:** `*` (not fixed; must be provided/selected)

- **IDS** (“Ident of secondary axis (A to Z)”)  
  Specifies the identifier of the secondary axis, stated as ranging from **A to Z**.  
  **Unit:** `LIT`  
  **Default:** `0`

- **SPT** (“offset for structural point numbers”)  
  Defines a numeric offset applied to structural point numbering when creating/using points for the secondary axis.  
  **Unit:** `—`  
  **Default:** `1`

- **GRP** (“offset for group numbers of GAXP”)  
  Defines an offset for group numbering specifically for **GAXP** placements tied to this secondary axis definition.  
  **Unit:** `—`  
  **Default:** `0`

- **Y** (“offset in transverse direction (local-y)”)  
  Specifies the transverse (horizontal) offset of the secondary axis relative to the primary axis, expressed in the local y-direction. This value may be constant, or conceptually be made variable via the mechanism described in the context (dependent on an axis variable via **GAXV**).  
  **Unit:** `m/Lit16`  
  **Default:** `0.0`

- **Z** (“offset in vertical direction (local-z)”)

  **Unit:** `m/Lit16`  
  **Default:** `0.0`

- **TILT** (“Designation of continuous beam”)  
  Provides a designation/reference for a continuous beam associated with this axis definition.  
  **Unit:** `Lit32`  
  **Default:** `-` (none)

Overall, GAXS is primarily a **geometric definition tool** for deriving a secondary axis location (via **Y** and **Z** offsets or via variable support with **GAXV**), plus **organizational controls** for point/group numbering offsets (**SPT**, **GRP**) and an optional beam association (**TILT**).
